description: **Python 3.14 required.** claudewheel now declares `requires-python >=3.14`; installers on Python 3.11 to 3.13 can no longer install new versions, and the npm launcher and `c` script refuse older interpreters.

**`claudewheel mv` no longer corrupts paths when the new name contains the old one.** With profiles sharing one session store, a move such as `foo` to `foobar` rewrote the transcripts once per profile, leaving `foobarbarbarbar` behind, and the dry-run counts were multiplied the same way. Each real session store is now processed once.

**Session data for projects whose path holds a space, `@`, `+`, or any other non-alphanumeric character is found again.** claudewheel now names a project's session directory exactly as Claude Code does, including the truncated, hash-suffixed name Claude Code uses for paths longer than 200 characters, so `mv`, `--resume`, `--cont`, and `import` look in the directory that actually holds the sessions.

**`claudewheel mv` moves session data left behind by deleted subprojects.** A session directory under the moved path whose project no longer exists and has no registry key is now identified by the working directory its own sessions recorded, and relabeled under the new path, so a move no longer refuses and nothing stays recorded under the old path. Every such directory is checked against registry keys, existing directories, and recorded working directories together, and a directory whose evidence names more than one path, or none, stops the move before anything changes.

**`claudewheel mv` refuses when a session file it must rewrite cannot be read.** It used to log the file and carry on, leaving that transcript at the old path while reporting success. The move now stops before changing anything and lists every unreadable file.

**`claudewheel mv` no longer leaves half-merged session directories behind.** When the old and new session directories both held a file of the same name, the move skipped it, printed a warning, and left the old directory in place. It now refuses before changing anything, naming both directories and the shared names, and any failure to remove the old directory after a merge stops the move with an error naming it.

**`--resume` reads a moved session's original directory correctly.** It used to take the first working directory a transcript recorded, which can be a directory the session merely visited, and then offered to move the wrong project or told you to run from the wrong place. It now uses the working directory whose name matches the session's directory, and refuses with an error when the transcripts record none or several.

**`claudewheel mv` no longer rewrites the paths of sibling projects inside session transcripts.** Moving `~/Projects/foo` used to change every `~/Projects/foobar` and `~/Projects/foo-bar` mentioned in the moved sessions as well, falsifying them into paths that never existed. A path is now moved only where it ends: at a `/`, a quote, whitespace, punctuation, or the end of the text; and fields that hold one path, such as a session's working directory or a tool's file path, move only when they are the moved path or lie inside it.

**`claudewheel import` reads each session's original directory correctly and refuses broken transcript links.** It used to take the first working directory a transcript recorded, which can be a directory the session merely visited, so sessions could be filed under the wrong project. It now uses the working directory whose name matches the session's directory, and refuses, naming the directory, when the transcripts record none or several. A session transcript in the source that is a symlink to a missing file used to be skipped with a warning; the import now refuses before writing anything and lists every such file.

**Memory-heavy commands must run through `heavy`.** A new hard-deny guardrail refuses test suites, large builds, and verification runs (`go test`, `go build`, `go vet`, `go install`, `pytest` in its `python -m` and `uv run` forms, `npm test`, `npm run test`, `npm ci`, `cargo test`, `cargo build`, `scripts/*test*.sh`, `scripts/full-suite.sh`, `cgofree generate`, and `cgofree verify`) wherever they start a command, including after `&&`, `;`, or a pipe and inside a subshell, and tells the agent to run `heavy -- <the command>` instead, with `--mem` for jobs needing more than 5G. The wrapped form is never refused. Profiles also get matching `deny` rules for the plain spellings the next time `claudewheel patch-profiles` runs.

**`claudewheel deploy-hooks` ships the `heavy` wrapper.** `heavy` runs a memory-heavy command alone on the machine and under a memory cap: one machine-wide lock queues heavy commands from every session, and each runs in its own systemd scope with a 5G limit (`--mem` changes it) and no swap, so a runaway job is killed alone instead of the whole terminal session. `deploy-hooks heavy` (or `--all`) writes it to `~/.claudewheel/scripts/heavy` and makes `~/.local/bin/heavy` a symlink to it; anything else already at that path is refused unless `--force-overwrite` is passed.

**Go toolchain builds and `make` must run through `heavy`.** The `heavy-unwrapped` guardrail now also refuses Go's own `./make.bash`, `./all.bash`, and `./run.bash` (by any path, or through `bash`/`sh`) and `make` wherever they start a command, and tells the agent to run `heavy -- <the command>` instead; the wrapped forms, such as `heavy -- ./all.bash` and `heavy -- make test`, are never refused. Profiles get matching `deny` rules for the plain spellings the next time `claudewheel patch-profiles` runs.

**`heavy` no longer leaks its lock, explains memory kills, and waits visibly and boundedly.** A process the command leaves running no longer keeps the machine-wide lock after `heavy` exits, which used to make every later `heavy` wait forever. When the command is killed for going over its memory cap, `heavy` says so and suggests a rerun with twice the cap (`heavy --mem 10G -- <command>`). Every run prints its cap, and a line when `-p=2` is added to `GOFLAGS`; the command runs at a lower CPU weight (20, against the default 100) so interactive work stays responsive. While waiting for the lock, `heavy` prints the holder and the time waited every 30 seconds, names a holder only while that process is still alive, and gives up with exit status 75 after 60 minutes (`--max-wait`, such as `90m` or `2h`, sets another limit), saying how to find and stop the holder. `--mem` without a value, or with a size that is not a whole number with a `K`, `M`, `G`, or `T` suffix, is a usage error. `claudewheel deploy-hooks` now replaces each script with a new file instead of rewriting it, so redeploying never disturbs a `heavy` or hook that is already running.

**`heavy` runs jobs side by side within a memory budget, replacing the one machine-wide lock.** Every heavy command declares its cap (`--mem`, 5G unless given), and starts once that cap, plus what the running heavy commands have not yet used of theirs, fits in the machine's available memory less a 2G margin; at most 8 run at once. A job that needs less, such as a single test or a small build, starts sooner with a smaller cap (`heavy --mem 2G -- <command>`), and a cap larger than the machine's memory less the margin is a usage error. A command whose `heavy` was killed keeps its cap reserved while it runs on, and the waiting message names the `systemctl --user stop` command that ends it. When the command returns, `heavy` stops whatever it left running. The command's arguments now reach it unchanged: `systemd-run` used to rewrite `$VAR` and `$$` in them, so `heavy -- bash -c 'echo $$'` printed `$`.

**Each session claudewheel launches runs in its own memory-capped systemd scope.** A memory-heavy command that runs outside `heavy` inside a session (a test suite inside `bash -c`, say) can now take down only its own session, not the whole terminal. The ceiling is `session_memory_max` in `config.json` (4G unless set) with `session_memory_swap_max` of swap (1G unless set, or `0`); claudewheel prints both at every launch, and a malformed value fails the launch naming the key. When the scope reaches its ceiling, the largest process in it is killed and the session carries on. `heavy` jobs started from a session are limited only by their own caps. `systemd-run` must be on the launch `PATH`. Sessions already running keep their old setup until they are relaunched.
heavy no longer waits out --max-wait for a cap that cannot fit while no heavy command is running; it exits at once (status 75) and names the largest cap that fits now.

**`heavy` no longer tells an agent to rerun a memory-killed command at twice the cap.** When a command is killed at its `--mem` cap, `heavy` names the peak before the kill and says not to rerun it with a bigger cap: a command that outgrows its cap is a defect to fix at the source. Only a cap that was a guess may be measured, once, at the largest cap that fits now, which `heavy` names. Every run now ends with the peak memory use of the command's scope, so a cap can be set from a measurement. The cannot-fit refusal and the give-up message no longer offer a guessed smaller `--mem` as the way around, and the give-up message names the `systemctl --user stop` of a stuck job's scope instead of a `kill` of its `heavy`, which left the command running and holding its cap.

**The `heavy-unwrapped` refusal no longer hands out guessed caps.** It used to suggest `heavy --mem 8G` for a bigger job and `heavy --mem 2G` for a smaller one; it now says `--mem` is set from the peak `heavy` prints when a command returns, that a command of unknown need is measured once with the largest cap that fits now, and that a command killed at its cap is a defect to fix at the source. Redeploy the hook scripts to pick it up.
